title: Monasteries
objective: After this level you can explain how monks copied books and kept learning alive.
summary: Benedict's Rule balanced prayer, work and reading. Monks copied books by hand in scriptoria, and Cassiodorus had his monks copy pagan classics too.

cards.headline: Scribes often said: “Two fingers hold the pen, but the whole body toils.”
cards.body: They knew. In the early Middle Ages, books found refuge in monasteries, and every one was copied by hand, letter by letter. So why were monks the ones holding the pens?

cards.headline: A rule for living
cards.body: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founded a monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy. He wrote a Rule for it that balanced prayer, work and study: about five hours of manual work and four of reading scripture and spiritual writings a day, with enough food and sleep. Moderate, as monastic life goes. By the early 9th century his Rule had replaced most others across northern and western Europe. One man’s timetable became a continent’s.

cards.headline: Why monks copied
cards.body: Benedict didn’t set out to build libraries. But monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, and the only way to get a book was to copy one. So monasteries set aside a writing room, the scriptorium, where scribes copied manuscripts onto parchment or vellum, made from animal skin. No printer, no photocopier: just a pen and a very long afternoon.

cards.headline: Saving the pagans
cards.body: Cassiodorus, who had served as a senior official under Theodoric (Level 3’s Gothic king of Italy), founded a monastery called Vivarium around 540. He had its monks copy pagan as well as Christian authors, and other monasteries later followed his example. It mattered, because books were scarce: a monastic library of 600 volumes counted as fairly large. A small-town library today would have looked like a miracle.
cards.callout: Copy it, or lose it: every book existed only as many times as someone wrote it out

mascot.line: If you remember one thing, make it this: every book existed only as a hand-made copy.

questions.prompt: What did the Rule of Saint Benedict balance in a monk’s day?

options.label: Fasting, silence and travel
options.rationale: Benedict allowed enough food and sleep.

questions.explanation: The Rule balanced prayer, work and study, including about five hours of manual work and four of reading.

questions.prompt: Why did early medieval monasteries copy so many books?

Kings paid them to write history for royal courts
Printing presses were banned inside monasteries
options.rationale: There were no printing presses yet.

options.label: Old books had to be copied to be sold abroad
options.rationale: They copied for use, not export.
